paperTitle: Singapore-Cambridge GCE O-Level 1184 English Language — AI-authored Practice 45: The Void Deck (§B style, standard band)
provenanceNote: NOT STUDENT-FACING. Original narrative written for the morning-quiz bank; NOT from any past exam paper. Section B [19 marks], 1184/02 §B format, SEAB assessment objectives. 10 short-answer items (mixed [1]/[2]) + 4-blank emotion flowchart split for independent auto-grading.

sections.instruction: Read the narrative text below about a boy who spends three nights at a neighbour's void-deck wake, and answer the questions that follow. Section B, Part 1 [15 marks]. Answer in your own words as far as possible.
sections.passage:
Paragraph 1
When Uncle Chandran died, they set up the wake in the void deck directly below our flat. For three nights the white tent stood where the old men usually played checkers, and the sound of it came up through our floor like weather.

Paragraph 2
My mother made me go down on the first evening. I had spoken to Uncle Chandran perhaps twice in my life — once when I kicked a ball into his corridor, and once when he asked me, in the lift, whether I was the one who played the guitar badly at night. I said I was. He said he did not mind.

Paragraph 3
I expected the wake to be unbearable. Instead there were plastic chairs, a folding table of peanuts and soft drinks, and about forty people who all seemed to know one another. Nobody cried where I could see them. An old woman near the front laughed at something and then covered her mouth.

Paragraph 4
His daughter stood by the entrance receiving people. She had flown in from Perth that morning; you could see the flight still on her. Each time somebody arrived she said the same three sentences, and each time she said them as though it were the first.

Paragraph 5
I sat at the back not knowing what to do with my hands. After a while a man in his sixties sat down beside me, took a handful of peanuts, and asked how I had known Chandran. I said I lived upstairs. He nodded as though this were a real answer and told me that in 1988 Uncle Chandran had lent him four hundred dollars and refused, for thirty-six years, to let him repay it.

Paragraph 6
Then somebody else told a story, and then somebody else. None of them were about anything large. He had fixed a gate. He had waited with a stranger's child at the clinic. He had, on one occasion, driven a woman to Johor at four in the morning and never explained why.

Paragraph 7
On the third night I went down without being told to. I did not stay long. I stood at the edge and listened to a man describe how Uncle Chandran had taught his son to ride a bicycle in the very space where the tent now stood, and I thought about the lift, and the guitar, and the fact that he had not minded.

Paragraph 8
The tent came down on Sunday morning. By noon the checkers table was back and two old men were arguing over it as though nothing had happened. That is how a void deck works. It holds whatever you put in it and then it lets go.

Paragraph 9
I still play badly at night. I have started leaving the window open when I do.

questions.stem: Q1. From Paragraph 1, where exactly was the wake held? [1]
questions.answer: in the void deck directly below the narrator's flat

questions.stem: Q2. What is the effect of the comparison of the sound of the wake to 'weather' (Paragraph 1)? [2]
questions.answer: it makes the wake feel like something large and impersonal happening to the whole block rather than to one family — unavoidable, filling the air, something the narrator lives underneath rather than takes part in

questions.stem: Q3. From Paragraph 2, give the TWO occasions on which the narrator had spoken to Uncle Chandran. [1]
questions.answer: when he kicked a ball into the corridor, and in the lift about his guitar playing

questions.stem: Q4. Using your own words, explain why the narrator found the wake different from what he had expected. (Paragraph 3) [2]
questions.answer: ① he had braced himself for open grief but found an ordinary, almost social gathering; ② the mood was warm and even light rather than unbearable

questions.stem: Q5. What does the detail of the old woman laughing 'and then covering her mouth' (Paragraph 3) suggest? [1]
questions.answer: she caught herself, feeling laughter was not permitted at a wake

questions.stem: Q6. What is the effect of the description of the daughter saying 'the same three sentences' as though it were the first time? (Paragraph 4) [2]
questions.answer: it shows her exhaustion and the mechanical strain of receiving mourner after mourner, while also showing her determination to give each person their due — the repetition exposes what the effort is costing her

questions.stem: Q7. Using your own words, explain what the story about the four hundred dollars reveals about Uncle Chandran. (Paragraph 5) [2]
questions.answer: ① he gave help without expecting anything back; ② his refusal over thirty-six years shows the generosity was a settled part of his character, not a single gesture

questions.stem: Q8. Using your own words, explain what the narrator comes to understand from the stories in Paragraph 6. [2]
questions.answer: ① a life is remembered through small ordinary kindnesses rather than notable achievements; ② these acts had reached people the narrator had never connected to his neighbour

questions.stem: Q9. What is significant about the narrator going down on the third night 'without being told to'? (Paragraph 7) [1]
questions.answer: he now goes by his own choice, out of genuine feeling rather than obligation

questions.stem: Q10. What is the effect of the closing detail that the narrator now leaves the window open when he plays? (Paragraph 9) [1]
questions.answer: it quietly honours Uncle Chandran, who had told him he did not mind the noise
